abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: In this study, we employed a method for evaluating dynamic exciton couplings by using atomic transition density moments and molecular dynamics (MD) coordinates. We then applied this computational approach to investigate protein-regulated exciton couplings in spinach light-harvesting complex II (LHCII). Our findings, based on a more realistic all-atom computational model in the presence of the photosystem II (PSII) core and minor antennas, reveal distinct coupling strength patterns for the monomers in LHCII. The probability distributions of excitonic couplings in isolated LHCII always exhibit a single peak, whereas those in the LHCII–PSII complex display a bimodal nature. Such reductions in the excitonic coupling strengths of the main pigments, especially for some chlorophyll–lutein pairs, suggest that the peripheral proteins could modulate energy transfer processes in LHCII–PSII. A closer examination of the key structural parameters reveals that the angles between helices A and B and the distance between CLA612 and LUT620 increase in LHCII–PSII, which are closely associated with the reductions in excitonic couplings.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
Almost all living beings on earth rely on the sun as a source of energy, and most solar energy is encapsulated in the chemical energy of biomass during the process of photosynthesis. More than that, photosynthesis can also produce molecular oxygen in the atmosphere, which is necessary for the majority of heterotrophic organisms. The photosystems distributed over thylakoid membranes of photosynthetic organisms (such as green plants and green algae) are the main sites for the ‘light reaction’. Light-harvesting complex II (LHCII), one of the most abundant membrane proteins in photosystem II, is a crucial component of the photosynthetic apparatus, playing a vital role in providing the initial driving force for photosynthesis. Despite the differences in structure and composition, LHCII always contains large ensembles of pigments that bind to the protein scaffolds. This special structure of LHCII ensures efficient absorption of the photosynthetically active radiation (400–740 nm) and then transfers the electronic excited energy to the reaction center. −
The efficient energy capture and delivery indeed help photosynthetic organisms to survive at very low levels of illumination, such as cloudy weather or water environments. , However, since the maximum turnover rate of the reaction center is slower than that of photon absorption and subsequent energy transfer in LHCII, photosynthetic organisms, especially land plants, face a formidable challenge once the solar radiation increases dramatically. Such a massive buildup of excitation energy in LHCII would lead to highly reactive species of radicals and singlet oxygen and then cause serious damage to photosystems, which is commonly known as ‘photoinhibition’. ,

To cope with the photodamage, photosynthetic organisms developed an effective defense, including a series of self-regulatory mechanisms. These reversible regulatory processes, called non-photochemical quenching (NPQ), usually involve several distinct components with very broad spatial and temporal scales. −
The fast and important NPQ is energy-dependent quenching, which can respond to the fluctuation of illumination within seconds to minutes and dissipate excessive excitation energy via nonradiative processes. −
However, the detailed mechanism of NPQ at the molecular level has not yet been elucidated, which remains an active research field currently. So far, several possible mechanisms were proposed to disclose the origin of the fast NPQ. −
Most studies ascribed the energy quenching to carotenoid molecules, since the short-lived dark excited state can directly take part in the NPQ process. , The strong electronic interaction between xanthophyll and chlorophyll was explained as the reason for the NPQ according to the experimental observations. Particularly, the short-lived S1 state of lutein (LUT) can be responsible for energy dissipation via a relatively slow energy transfer from the S1 (Q y ) state adjacent chlorophylls. , Theoretically, quantum chemistry is a powerful approach to elucidate the excitonic dynamics in LHCII, such as an exciton picture combined with a quantum master equation. , Three fundamental parameters of site energies, excitonic couplings, and spectral densities directly govern the resonance energy transfer rate in excitonic dynamics.

Herein, several theoretical studies on excitonic couplings will follow in terms of high-resolution crystal structures of photosystems. −
Novoderezhkin et al. modeled excitonic interactions between chlorophylls according to the dipole–dipole approximation. , Müh and co-workers considered the effects of a realistic environment and calculated the excitonic couplings of chlorophyll pairs in LHCII. , However, they did not study the chlorophyll–xanthophyll excitonic interactions due to difficulties in modeling the strongly correlated 2Ag– state of carotenoids. Duffy et al. made the first attempt to clarify the fluorescence quenching by computing excitonic couplings between chlorophyll and xanthophyll via atomic transition density moments. Later, they performed a more general model for excitonic coupling calculations that contains all pigments with the transition density cube method. They found that the LUT molecule could be responsible for the energy quenching rather than violaxanthin and neoxanthin in LHCII. Recently, the excitonic couplings of the chlorophyll–LUT pair were also estimated by high-level CASSCF and RASSCF formulations. In addition, several MD studies were conducted to investigate the allosteric regulation of LHCII under various external stimuli, such as pH gradients and ionic conditions, in order to elucidate the variations in excitonic couplings and the transitions between light-harvesting and energy-quenched states. −
For example, Croce et al. carried out MD simulations to identify the structural changes between the light-harvesting and energy quenching along with the evolution of interpigment couplings. Duffy et al. further figured out the critical structural parameters for controlling the chlorophyll–carotenoid interactions. Daskalakis et al. explored the conformational phase space of LHCII and identified key residues and structural changes that influence excitonic couplings in chlorophyll–carotenoid pairs. ,

Although more and more understandings on the excitonic couplings in LHCII have been revealed based on theoretical studies, the existing computational models are still far from perfect, with limitations such as the absence of the PSII core and other minor antennas and the conventional omission of phytol tails in chlorophylls. In this work, we aim to address the above shortcomings of molecular modeling to provide a more realistic representation of the protein environment. We will focus on the roles of the PSII core and other minor antennas, which may create an anisotropic protein environment around three monomers, regulate excitonic coupling strengths, and potentially influence the allosteric regulation of LHCII. We believe that this work can not only propose a better computational model to study excitonic couplings in proteins but also provide new knowledge of the energy transfer process of photosynthesis.

sec.title: System Modeling
sec.p: The crystal structure of spinach LHCII–PSII supercomplex (PDB ID: 3JCU) at 3.2 Å resolution was adopted to build up the system in our MD simulations. First, the exogenous molecules of diglyceride, alkyl chains, detergents, and glycerol introduced during experiments were removed. Then the Modeler in the Chimera suite was used to fix the missing atoms and side chains of proteins. , The phytol tails of chlorophyll a (CLA) and chlorophyll b (CHL) were repaired by tLEaP in AmberTools and were checked manually. Later, the protonation states of His, Asp, and Glu were automatically determined using the H++ Web site (pH = 7.5) and were examined manually, especially for His in coordination with Heme-b (HEM), CLA, and CHL to maintain the reasonable structures. The LHCII–PSII supercomplex was embedded into a lipid bilayer with 1848 DOPC molecules using the membrane builder of CHARMM-GUI. As shown in Figures a and c, the final system was solvated in a water box (302.0 Å × 302.3 Å × 154.0 Å) containing 340,804 waters and neutralized by inserting 138 sodium ions (totally 1,429,924 atoms). Following a similar procedure, we also constructed isolated LHCII (Figures b and d), which was extracted from the spinach LHCII–PSII supercomplex. The simulation box (121.3 Å × 121.3 Å × 99.5 Å) includes 151,095 atoms in total with 306 DOPC, 30,713 waters, and 30 sodium ions. The distribution patterns of different pigments within a monomer of LHCII can be seen in Figure . Notably, the crystal structure of LHCII usually represents a highly energy-quenched state, while the light-harvesting state may be obtained under a relatively high pH. Starting from the crystallographic data, we adjusted the pH to 7.5 and thus may capture pronounced structural changes between pigments due to the allosteric regulation of LHCII. For comparison, several dynamic simulations were also conducted for LHCII–PSII under low pH conditions , and realistic salt conditions. In addition, It is also important to emphasize that the standard DOPC lipids were used in the current study, rather than native thylakoid lipids, which may have a certain influence on the simulations.

sec.p: The proteins and ions were modeled with the all-atom Amber03 force field during the MD simulations. The Amber lipid17 force field in the CHARMM-GUI program was adopted for the DOPC lipids. The TIP3P model was applied to water solvents. The force field parameters developed by Zhang et al. were chosen for six cofactors of CLA, CHL, HEM, pheophytin A (PHO), β-carotene (BCR), and plastoquinone A (PL9), and those for various carotenoids of XAT, LUT, and NEX were taken from the previous work by Prandi et al. The antechamber (GAFF2) in AmberTools was used to generate the force field parameters for bicarbonate ion (BCT). For the OEX complex (CaMn4O5), the atomic charges were assigned to Mn1–Mn4 as +3, O1–O5 as −2, and Ca as +2; the harmonic restraints with a force constant of 2.261 × 105 kJ·mol–1·nm–2 were also added between metal atoms and the coordinated protein residues in order to maintain a reasonable coordination structure around the OEX complex. This strategy has been applied successfully by Zhang et al. to model the crystal structure of PSII at 1.9 Å resolution. ,

sec.title: MD Simulations
sec.p: The LHCII–PSII supercomplex system was divided into four active components: cofactors, proteins, DOPC lipids, water molecules, and ions. Initially, we performed a step-by-step energy minimization using the steepest descent algorithm (10,000 steps) for each active component while freezing the remaining parts. The entire system was then further energy minimized for another 10,000 steps without any positional restraints or constraints. Next, the system was heated under an NVT ensemble, with position restraints applied to all heavy atoms of the LHCII–PSII supercomplex. Specifically, a series of MD simulations, each of which lasts for 100 ps, were performed at 50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 K, followed by a 500 ps simulation at 300 K. Subsequently, an NPT pre-equilibration process was implemented with positional restraints that were removed gradually (from 0 to 100 ps: force constant of 3000 kJ·mol–1·nm–2 for proteins and pigments and 1000 kJ·mol–1·nm–2 for the lipid membrane; from 100 to 200 ps: 3000 kJ·mol–1·nm–2 for proteins and pigments and 500 kJ·mol–1·nm–2 for the lipid membrane; from 200 to 400 ps: 250 kJ·mol–1·nm–2 for proteins, pigments, and the lipid membrane; from 400 to 600 ps: 100 kJ·mol–1·nm–2 for proteins, pigments, and the lipid membrane; from 600 to 900 ps: no additional restraints).

During the final NPT MD production, all of the positional restraints were removed. For LHCII, the simulation was propagated straightforwardly for 1 μs. For LHCII–PSII at a much larger size, the simulation was first performed for 100 ns. Then snapshots at 96, 98, and 100 ns were selected as the initial conditions for three independent MD simulations. Each simulation was executed for 300 ns, providing a total of 0.9 μs MD sampling for data collection and analysis. The results of structural stability analysis are shown in Figures S1 and S2. The particle mesh Ewald approach was adopted for long-range electrostatic interactions. The velocity-rescaling thermostat and the Parrinello–Rahman barostat , were used to maintain the temperature at 300 K and the pressure at 1 atm, respectively. The covalent hydrogen bonds were constrained using the LINCS algorithm. All MD simulations were carried out using the Gromacs 5.4.1 program.

sec.title: Excited State Calculations
sec.p: The semiempirical calculations were conducted in the MNDO program (version 8.0). This MNDO/MRCI method can give a balanced description of the ground and excited states for LUT, CLA, and CHL, especially for the vertical excitation energies and the relevant electronic configurations. The restricted open-shell Hartree–Fock formalism was adopted in the self-consistent-field calculations. For xanthophyll LUT, 10 conjugated π and π* orbitals along the carbon chain (including four highest doubly occupied orbitals, four lowest unoccupied orbitals, and two singly occupied orbitals) were chosen as the active space in the MRCI calculations (Figure S3). For CLA and CHL, the active space in MRCI was composed of 18 π and π* orbitals, namely, eight highest doubly occupied orbitals, eight lowest unoccupied orbitals, and two singly occupied orbitals (Figures S4 and S5). For the MRCI treatment, three electronic configurations derived from the HOMO and LUMO orbitals of the closed-shell ground state were chosen as references. The MRCI wave function was built by allowing single, double, and triple excitations for LUT and single and double excitations for CLA and CHL. Additionally, we included a concise description of the complete active space self-consistent-field (CASSCF) and multistate second-order perturbation theory (MS-CASPT2) methods in the Supporting Information, specifying an active space of 10 electrons in 8 orbitals (Figure S6). Further details can be found in our previous work.

sec.title: Computation Procedure
sec.p:
The whole procedure of our calculations in this work can be summarized as follow. After validation, the transition density moments T
i of LUT, CLA, and CHL were computed with eqs S8–S16 (Table S2), in which the atomic orbital coefficients and electronic configurations were obtained from excited-state electronic structure calculations. Long-time ground-state MD simulations were performed for both LHCII and LHCII–PSII, with snapshots saved every 50 ps. The atomic coordinates of LUT, CLA, and CHL extracted from equilibrium snapshots were applied to eq . Finally, the intermolecular excitonic couplings were evaluated according to eq , using V
ij and T
i computed for LUT, CLA, and CHL. It is worth noting that the present method is advantageous over the widely used dipole model because the molecular structures of the donor and acceptor have been considered at the atomic scale, but the impacts of external environment and geometry change on the transition density moments of the donor and acceptor are still ignored.

sec.title: Key Structural Parameters
sec.p: In order to analyze the relationship between the interpigment excitonic couplings in LHCII and the variations of protein structures during MD simulations, we selected two pairs of the most significant and representative exciton couplings, CLA611–CLA612 and CLA612–LUT620, to identify the key structural parameters that determine excitonic coupling strengths. The relevant structural parameters that control the position and orientation of the pigment pairs can be seen in Figures b and c. First, the plane of chlorophyll is constituted by the chlorin ring, and the geometric centers are identified as the center of the chlorin ring (for CLA and CHL) or the center of the conjugated carbon skeleton (for LUT). Then the distance is defined as the length between two geometric centers; the dislocation angle refers to the angle between the normal vector of the chlorophyll plane and the line connecting the geometric centers of chlorophyll and LUT; the dihedral angle describes the angle between the two chlorin rings of chlorophylls; and the rotation angles of R1­(C1C2C4C3), R2­(C3C4C6C5), and R3­(C5C6C8C7) indicate the rotational degree of the conjugated carbon skeleton of LUT.

sec.title: MNDO/MRCI Calculations
sec.p: Previously, we proved that the OM2/MRCI structural optimization combined with single-point energy calculation at the MS-CASPT2­(10,8)/6-31G­(d) computational level can reasonably model the strongly correlated S1 state of xanthophyll LUT. However, the missing semiempirical parameters of the Mg element in OM2/MRCI prevent us from calculating the ground- and excited-state properties of CLA and CHL. In this work, the MNDO/MRCI method was adopted to calculate the S1 state of CLA, CHL, and LUT. As listed in Tables and , the MNDO/MRCI and MS-CASPT2 methods can provide very similar electronic configurations and vertical excitation energies for the S1 and S2 states of LUT. The S2 state provided here is only used for comparison with the available experimental value of LUT. For example, the vertical excitation energy of the S2(1Bu+) state is 2.67 and 2.68 eV at MNDO/MRCI and MS-CASPT2, which is about 0.1 eV the absorption maximum (2.59 eV) of LUT in the experiment in hexane. The optically dark properties of the S1 state make it impossible to directly extract the vertical excitation properties from the absorption spectrum experiments. The dark S1(2Ag–) state of LUT has a major double electronic excitation in which two electrons in the HOMO are promoted to the LUMO. The vertical excitation energies of this dark state were calculated to be 2.49 and 2.47 eV using MNDO/MRCI and MS-CASPT2, respectively, which are much higher than Walla and co-workers’ measured value of 1.78 eV by the two-photon absorption spectrum in solution. The inconsistency between experiments and calculations comes from the difficulty inherent in modeling the strongly correlated property of the S1 state theoretically. Many other theoretical studies on the S1(2Ag–) state of LUT also gave similar results, such as 2.87 eV by DSRG-MRPT2, 2.19 eV by R-AM1/FOMO-CASCI, and 2.13 eV by DFT/MRCI, which are also higher than the experimental measurement. −

sec.p: As for CLA and CHL, the MNDO/MRCI method can also provide reliable S1 vertical excitation energies of 1.98 and 2.05 eV, which is in good agreement with the experimental value of 1.93 and 1.98 eV. The TDA-CAM-B3LYP/def2-TZVP calculations were computed using Gaussian16, providing much higher vertical excitation energies of 2.28 and 2.36 eV for CLA and CHL. All these methods predicted that the chlorophylls’ S1 state is a bright state, which originates from the HOMO to LUMO transition.

Notably, Götze et al. pointed out that the vertical excitation energies (VH and VG) are often higher than experimental peaks because experiments capture vibrationally relaxed states. For CLA and CHL, the 0–0 transition dominates, so vertical excitation energies closely match experiments, consistent with our present calculations. For LUT, VH and VG give 0–0 transition energies of 2.29 and 2.67 eV, while the adiabatic (AH) value of 2.49 eV aligns better with experiments. This phenomenon is mainly caused by the combined effect of the reorganization energy and ground state destabilization. Overall, the MNDO/MRCI method can be a reasonable choice for calculating the S1 state of LUT, CLA, and CHL and is also suitable for computing excitonic couplings.

sec.title: Excitonic Coupling Calculations
sec.p:
As mentioned in eq , excitonic coupling J
DA can be obtained from transition density moments T
i (calculated with MNDO/MRCI) and coefficients V
ij (extracted from MD trajectories). The initial excitonic couplings of monomer 1 in LHCII were first calculated to validate our computational model. The interpigment couplings of one monomer in spinach LHCII (PDB code: 1RWT) were estimated from the static crystal configuration by Duffy and Müh and are collected in Table S3, and our calculated initial excitonic couplings of monomer 1 in LHCII (PDB code: 3JCU) are listed in the top panel of Table S4 (upper-right triangle). We further depict the absolute values of excitonic couplings and coupling differences between our computations and those calculated by Duffy and Müh in Figure . The calculated couplings of the initial structure of monomer 1 in LHCII are basically consistent with those computed by Duffy using MNDO-CAS-CI and by Müh using TD-DFT. Most of the coupling differences are less than 3.0 cm–1 except for a small proportion larger than 10.0 cm–1. The CLA611–CLA612 pair with the largest coupling value was computed to be 103.1 cm–1 by us, 131.4 cm–1 by Duffy, and 99.0 cm–1 by Müh. The coupling between CLA612 and LUT620 is 13.4 cm–1, in good agreement with Duffy’s result of 12.2 cm–1, and that of CLA603-LUT621 herein is about half of the value of Duffy et al. The inconsistency in excitonic couplings may arise from two factors: first, the different crystal structures used in our system modeling (PDB ID: 3JCU) and the one used by Duffy and Müh (PDB ID: 1RWT), which might introduce anisotropy issues during sampling, as crystal packing effects can influence protein structures and conformations. Second, the inclusion of phytol tails in CLA and CHL during molecular modeling might also contribute to the discrepancies. Overall, our calculation model can give reasonable excitonic coupling strengths for pigments in LHCII.

sec.title: Excitonic Couplings in LHCII
sec.p: Previously, Duffy and co-workers assumed that excitonic couplings of different pigments in each monomer of LHCII are equivalent. In this work, we calculated the excitonic couplings of monomers 1, 2, and 3 in LHCII separately and found that three monomers do share very similar coupling strengths at the optimized static minimum structure (Figure ). The CLA611–CLA612 pair in the strongly coupled chlorophyll terminal emitter of CLA610–CLA611–CLA612 exhibits the largest excitonic coupling in all of the monomers. But there are still a few differences. For example, the CLA602–CLA603 and CLA613–CLA614 pairs in monomer 3 exhibit stronger coupling strengths compared to the corresponding pigment pairs in monomers 1 and 2. In contrast, the larger coupling for the CLA611–CLA612 pair is observed in monomer 2 than those in monomers 1 and 3.

caption.p: Absolute interpigment excitonic couplings (in cm–1) of monomers 1 (M1), 2 (M2), and 3 (M3) in LHCII.

sec.p: Up to now, the excitonic couplings were obtained from the optimized static structure, which appear to be insufficient to accurately capture the fluctuations occurring within a realistic protein environment. Their probability distributions obtained from MD simulations are displayed in Figure . For CLA611–CLA612, the average excitonic couplings are 102.1 and 100.8 cm–1 for monomers 1 and 2, respectively, and decrease to 87.0 cm–1 in monomer 3; monomer 3 exhibits a relatively broader distribution compared to that of monomers 1 and 2, ranging from 50.0 to 125.0 cm–1. The average couplings of CLA603–LUT621 in monomers 1 and 2 were computed to be 7.3 and 7.5 cm–1, while those in monomer 3 were estimated to be 8.6 cm–1. The same tendency was observed for CLA612-LUT620 with the coupling strengths of 13.7, 13.1, and 9.5 cm–1 in monomers 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Taking protein fluctuations into account, the excitonic couplings of monomers 1 and 2 show very similar strengths, while monomer 3 displays a slightly different coupling pattern.

sec.title: Time Evolution of Excitonic Couplings and Structural Parameters
sec.p: As displayed in Figure , the excitonic couplings of CLA611–CLA612 in monomers 1 and 2 vary slightly over time, while those in monomer 3 undergo relatively large changes in LHCII. We further picked out three representative snapshots with different structural parameters of monomer 3 in LHCII (Figure c). The first snapshot was selected at ∼270 ns with the excitonic coupling of ∼70.0 cm–1, in which the distance between CLA611–CLA612, the dislocation angle, and the dihedral angle were 10.5 Å, 65°, and 26°, respectively. The distance became smaller after 400 ns, especially at ∼760 ns, with the distance of 8.0 Å. Simultaneously, the excitonic coupling increased to ∼115.0 cm–1. At ∼950 ns, the distance and the dislocation angle increased, but the dihedral angle was reduced. The comprehensive effect of structural changes led to a slight decrease in exciton coupling (∼108.0 cm–1). In addition, remarkable motion of the phytol tails in CLA can be observed during MD simulations. As shown in Figure d, the orientation of the phytol tails initially paralleled the chlorine ring and then became angled, potentially affecting the position and excitonic coupling of the CLA611–CLA612 pair.

caption.p: Time evolution of excitonic couplings and key structural parameters of CLA611–CLA612 in monomers 1 (a), 2 (b), and 3 (c), along with representative snapshots in monomer 3 (d) (indicated by green stars).

sec.p: The excitonic couplings of CLA612–LUT620 are 1 order of magnitude smaller than those of CLA611–CLA612. The long and flexible carbon skeleton makes the LUT molecule easy to deform and hinders us from defining a stable plane for LUT. Instead, we employed three rotation angles (R1, R2, and R3) along the conjugated carbon skeleton rather than the dihedral angle between two planes to describe the geometrical structure of CLA612–LUT620. As shown in Figure , the excitonic coupling between CLA612 and LUT620 in monomers 1 and 2 remained at a stable geometry and fluctuated around ∼13.0 cm–1. In contrast, CLA612–LUT620 in monomer 3 presented large-amplitude fluctuations of excitonic couplings and structural parameters (Figure c). The separation of CLA and LUT became larger between 450 and 800 ns, and the rotation angle of R1/R2/R3 varies from 2.0°/176.0°/8.7° at 510 ns to 5.2°/149.4°/46.9° at 880 ns, indicating a deformation of LUT. The geometric changes may induce fluctuations of excitonic couplings and reduce the averaged coupling strength to ∼7.5 cm–1. Based on the time evolution of excitonic couplings, it is conceivable that LUT binds more tightly to proteins than the CLA and CHL molecules, since the structural changes of CLA611–CLA612 are much easier than those of CLA612–LUT620. It is consistent with Duffy’s work, in which both LUTs are rigidly fixed position-wise relative to their chlorophyll partners. As a result, the coupling magnitude of CLA612–LUT620 exhibits smaller amplitude oscillations. Notably, the selected structural parameters can only partially characterize the variations of exciton couplings within the system. Many other complicated factors, such as deplanarization of the chlorin ring, may also play significant roles.

caption.p: Time evolution of excitonic couplings and key structural parameters of CLA612–LUT620 in monomers 1 (a), 2 (b), and 3 (c), along with representative snapshots in monomer 3 (d) (indicated by green stars).

sec.title: Excitonic Couplings in LHCII–PSII
sec.p: We further focus on potential effects of the PSII core and minor antennae of CP26 and CP29 on the excitonic couplings in LHCII. The probability distributions of absolute excitonic couplings of representative pigment pairs in the LHCII–PSII supercomplex are shown in Figure . Compared to the isolated LHCII, most probability distributions of excitonic couplings exhibit a bimodal character in LHCII–PSII. In monomers 1 and 2, additional peaks with much weaker coupling strengths (22.9 and 10.6 cm–1 for CLA611–CLA612; 5.3 and 1.4 cm–1 for CLA612–LUT620) can be observed. Although stronger couplings for CLA603–LUT621 also appear in LHCII–PSII (e.g., 10.3 and 11.2 cm–1 in monomers 1 and 3), the corresponding averaged values are close to that in isolated LHCII on account of another peak with smaller strengths (e.g., 1.5 and 7.2 cm–1 in monomers 1 and 3). Overall, the couplings in monomer 2 decrease more significantly than those in monomer 1, while monomer 3 undergoes the smallest change, indicating that the PSII core and the minor antennas of CP26 and CP29 may provide an anisotropic chemical environment to different monomers.

Again, the probability distributions of excitonic couplings in LHCII exhibit a single peak, whereas those in LHCII–PSII display a bimodal nature. As a result, the overall excitonic couplings in LHCII–PSII become much smaller than those in LHCII. For example, the averaged couplings of CLA612–LUT620 were calculated as 12.1 and 6.9 cm–1 in isolated LHCII and LHCII–PSII, respectively.

sec.p: To evaluate the potential influence of different MD protocols on conformational sampling and excitonic couplings, we performed three additional MD simulations of LHCII–PSII under (1) standard conditions (650 ns duration), (2) low pH, and (3) realistic salt conditions. The relevant results are presented in Figures S7–S9. On one hand, the bimodal excitonic coupling pattern was still observed, and the key conclusion remains unchanged in (1) and (3). On the other hand, in (2), the bimodal nature of excitonic couplings nearly disappears, replaced by a unimodal distribution. This indicates that low pH stabilizes the LHCII–PSII structure in the photoprotective state. More details can be seen in the Supporting Information.

sec.title: Comparison with Previous Works
sec.p: As mentioned above, the distinct excitonic coupling patterns differ between the LHCII and LHCII–PSII complexes, exhibiting single-peak versus bimodal spectral features, respectively. This difference motivates a comparative analysis of their protein scaffolds and pigment molecules in comparison to previous works.

Recently, Weng and co-workers investigated the distribution of the strength of excitonic couplings between LUT and chlorophylls in LHCII using multistate DFT and MD simulations at different conditions. Additionally, they also explored the quantum switch between light-harvesting and energy-quenching states in plants using a combination of multistate DFT along with X-ray and cryo-EM structures, in which both Dexter and Förster mechanisms are included and determined explicitly. They stated that nanodiscs can provide a lateral constraint force to the LHCII trimer (pH 5.4) and prompt the system to the energy-quenching state. In this state, the angles of LUT620–LUT621 and helices A and B were estimated to range from 73.2° to 77.1° and from 116.4° to 117.8°, respectively. Based on the measured rates, a critical distance of 5.6 Å between CLA612 and LUT620 was inferred to be the turning point between Förster and Dexter mechanisms. At pH 7.8 in solvent, they further observed that the angles of LUT620–LUT621 and helices A and B in LHCII increased to ∼80° and ∼120°, respectively, and the distance between CLA612 and LUT620 also became larger, suggesting a dynamic switch to a light-harvesting state.

As mentioned above, we started from a highly energy-quenched crystal structure and adjusted the pH to 7.5 in order to partially capture pronounced structural changes between pigments due to the allosteric regulation of LHCII. According to the initial structure for our simulations, the angles of LUT620–LUT621 and helices A and B, as well as the distance between CLA612 and LUT620, were in the range of 60.0–65.0°, 112.0–116.0°, and 6.10–6.50 Å, respectively. It indicates an energy-quenching state and qualitatively agrees with the observations by Ruan et al. in nanodiscs. We further extracted representative structures of monomers 1, 2, and 3 from production NPT MD trajectories. The results of LHCII–PSII can be seen in Figure . Most of the relevant angles and distances increased during simulations with the average values being 65.9°, 118.6°, and 9.17 Å for monomer 1, 67.2°, 119.9°, and 10.03 Å for monomer 2, and 64.0°, 116.5°, and 7.02 Å for monomer 3, respectively. A careful comparison between representative structures and the CLA612–LUT620 excitonic couplings reveals that the structural changes may correspond to the additional peaks of J DA’s distribution in the presence of the PSII core and minor antennas (see Figures g–i). Representative structures of isolated LHCII are shown in Figure . It can be seen that the averaged distances between CLA612 and LUT620 in all monomers decreased below 7.0 Å; the averaged angle of helices A and B between 108.8° and 113.3° became closer to its initial value rather than that in LHCII–PSII. These structural parameters suggest that the isolated LHCII remains consistently trapped in the energy-quenched state throughout 1 μs MD simulations.

sec.p: Overall, the tendency of structural changes in the presence of the PSII core and minor antennas is consistent with the previous work by Ruan et al. Based on the above comparison and analysis, we speculated that peripheral proteins may provide an anisotropic protein environment to LHCII. Additionally, the variation in the protein scaffold, specifically the angle between helices A and B, seems to be relevant to the excitonic couplings in LHCII–PSII by affecting the angle between LUT620 and LUT621 and the distance between CLA612 and LUT620. The larger angle between helices A and B, as well as the increased distance between pigments, may result in a bimodal distribution of excitonic couplings within LHCII–PSII and finally reduce the coupling strengths, particularly between CLA612 and LUT620.

More recently, Mennucci et al. discovered that the second dihedral angle, located on the lumenal side, of the LUT molecule plays a pivotal role in determining the s-cis or s-trans conformation, which may influence both light-harvesting efficiency and photoprotection in plant antenna complexes. In LHCII, the s-cis conformation of LUT at the L2 site enhances light absorption by lowering the excitation energy, while the s-trans conformation at the L1 site is optimized for photoprotection.

To further clarify the distinct roles of the two LUT molecules, we conducted a detailed conformational analysis in our MD simulations, both in isolated LHCII and in the LHCII–PSII supercomplex. As shown in Figure S10, both LUT620 and LUT621 in isolated LHCII adopt the s-trans conformation, which favors the photoprotective state, consistent with our previous discussions (Figure ). However, in monomer 2 of LHCII–PSII, LUT620 transiently adopts an s-cis conformation but quickly reverts to the s-trans state (Figure S11). Furthermore, we analyzed the relationship between this dihedral transition and excitonic coupling. As illustrated in Figure S12, our findings indicate that the second dihedral angle does not exhibit a direct correlation with the reduction in excitonic couplings. This is consistent with recent studies by Mennucci and co-workers, , which show that the excitonic couplings between LUT and chlorophylls in CP29 are minimally affected by the s-trans/s-cis conformational change of LUT, and the Coulomb interactions between LUT and chlorophylls remain insensitive to protein conformational rearrangements. Instead, the coupling appears to be influenced primarily by the distance between the LUT and chlorophylls, at least within the scope of our current simulations (Figure S12).

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In the present work, we constructed a more realistic computational model to study protein-regulated exciton couplings in spinach LHCII. All-atom MD simulations combined with semiempirical MNDO/MRCI electronic structure calculations were performed to estimate the coupling strengths of key pigments in isolated LHCII and the LHCII–PSII supercomplex. In the case of isolated LHCII, the three monomers are nearly equivalent, sharing similar coupling patterns. In the presence of the PSII core and minor antennas, the probability distribution of excitonic couplings changes from a single peak to a bimodal nature, leading to remarkably reduced coupling strengths between CLA611 and CLA612, CLA612 and LUT620, and CLA603 and LUT621. We further analyzed the time evolution of excitonic couplings and protein structures and compared the present computational results to recent experiments by Weng and co-workers. It suggests that the peripheral proteins may provide an anisotropic protein environment to LHCII, which could affect the excitonic couplings between the pigments in LHCII–PSII. Our findings underscore the importance of the PSII core and minor antennas in molecular modeling of the light-harvesting complex and highlight the limitations of excitonic couplings derived from the isolated LHCII structures.
